title: Ticketing systems: ServiceNow, Jira & Zendesk
monthTitle: The Helpdesk Professional: ITIL, Ticketing & Soft Skills
summary: Learn how IT ticketing systems work and how to write a clean, complete ticket in the three platforms you are most likely to meet on the job.
objectives: Explain what a ticketing system is and why every service desk uses one
Describe the lifecycle of a ticket from New to Closed
Identify the core fields every ticket should contain
Compare ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, and Zendesk at a high level
Write a clear, well-structured ticket that another technician could pick up
Use ticket categories, priority, and assignment correctly

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a ticketing system?
options: To track, manage, and document every support request in one place
quiz.why: A ticketing system records each request, tracks its status, and keeps a complete history so nothing is lost and work can be measured and audited.

quiz.q: Which sequence best represents a typical ticket lifecycle?
quiz.why: Tickets generally flow New, then In Progress (often via On Hold/Pending), to Resolved once fixed, and finally Closed after confirmation.

quiz.q: Which platform is an IT service management suite most associated with large enterprises?
quiz.why: ServiceNow is a large, enterprise-focused ITSM platform; Zendesk leans toward customer support and Jira toward dev-aligned teams, though all three handle IT tickets.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid a ticket subject like 'It's broken'?
options: It gives no information, so the ticket can't be triaged or searched
quiz.why: A vague subject can't be categorised, prioritised, or found later; a good subject names the system and the symptom, e.g. 'Outlook - password incorrect error'.

quiz.q: List the core fields every well-formed ticket should contain.
quiz.answer: Requester/user, contact details, a clear subject, a detailed description with symptoms and timing, category, priority, and the assignment or queue.
quiz.why: These fields let any technician triage, prioritise, and pick up the ticket without having to chase the user for basics.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why does good ticket hygiene matter to the whole team?
quiz.answer: Clean, complete tickets mean any technician can pick up the work without re-interviewing the user, which speeds resolution and builds a searchable knowledge history.
quiz.why: Tickets are shared records; sloppy ones create rework, while well-written ones become future knowledge-base material.

body_markdown:
## Why every service desk uses a ticketing system

A **ticketing system** is the shared workspace where every support request is logged, tracked, and documented. Without one, requests scatter across inboxes, sticky notes, and hallway conversations — and things get lost. With one, every contact becomes a **ticket** with an ID, a status, a history, and an owner. It is the source of truth for the whole team.

Ticketing systems also make work *measurable*. Because every request is recorded, the desk can report on volumes, response times, and recurring problems.

## The lifecycle of a ticket

Every ticket moves through **states**. The names vary slightly by platform, but the shape is the same:

```text
New  ->  In Progress  ->  (On Hold / Pending)  ->  Resolved  ->  Closed
```

- **New** — logged but not yet picked up.
- **In Progress** — a technician is actively working it.
- **On Hold / Pending** — waiting on the user, a vendor, or a part.
- **Resolved** — the fix is applied; awaiting confirmation.
- **Closed** — confirmed fixed and finished.

Never skip states. The status field tells everyone — including the user — exactly where things stand.

## The fields that make a ticket usable

A ticket another technician can pick up cold contains:

- **Requester** and **contact details**
- A specific **subject** naming the system and symptom
- A **description** with symptoms, error text, timing, and what changed
- **Category** (e.g. Email, Network, Hardware)
- **Priority**
- **Assignment** to a person or queue

Compare these two subjects:

```text
Bad:  It's broken
Good: Outlook 365 - "password incorrect" error since 09:00 today
```

The good subject can be triaged, searched, and understood in one glance.

## The three platforms you will meet

Three tools dominate the job market:

| Platform | Strength | Typical home |
|----------|----------|--------------|
| **ServiceNow** | Full enterprise ITSM, ITIL-aligned | Large organisations |
| **Jira Service Management** | Tight link to dev teams, flexible | Software-driven companies |
| **Zendesk** | Friendly, fast, omnichannel | Customer-support-heavy teams |

The good news: they all share the same core concepts. Learn the lifecycle and field discipline once, and you can move between them quickly. The buttons differ; the thinking does not.

## Writing the ticket

When you log a contact, capture the user's words *and* the technical facts. A clean description reads like a short report:

```text
User reports Outlook prompts "password incorrect" repeatedly
since ~09:00. Webmail login works with same password.
No recent password change reported. Laptop, Windows 11, on VPN.
Verified account is not locked in directory.
```

That description tells the next person what was tried and rules things out — it is half the troubleshooting already done.

## Your task

Write a complete ticket for this scenario: a user named Sam in Finance reports that the shared accounting drive 'S:' disappeared from their PC after a reboot this morning; other users can still see it. Include subject, category, priority, and a description with symptoms, timing, and what you have already verified. Aim for the quality of the 'Good' examples above.

slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson we get hands-on with the single most important tool on any service desk: the ticketing system. We'll look at how tickets flow from start to finish, the fields that make a ticket genuinely usable, and the three platforms you're most likely to meet on the job, which are ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, and Zendesk. By the end you'll be able to write a ticket any technician could pick up.

slides.narration: When you write the description, capture both the user's words and the technical facts. A clean description reads like a short report. Notice in this example how it states what was tried, what was ruled out, and the environment, the operating system, the device, the network. A description like that tells the next person exactly where things stand. In a real sense, a good description is half the troubleshooting already done for whoever picks it up.

slides.title: Category, priority, assignment
bullets: Category routes the ticket to the right team.
Priority sets the order of work.
Assignment names the owner or queue.
Get these right and triage takes seconds.
slides.narration: Three more fields tie it all together. The category, like Email, Network, or Hardware, routes the ticket to the right team. The priority sets the order in which work gets done, which we'll cover in detail in a later lesson. And the assignment names the owner, whether that's a person or a queue. When these three are filled in correctly, triage takes seconds and the ticket lands in exactly the right hands the first time.

slides.narration: Let's recap. Ticketing systems are the shared source of truth, and every request becomes a ticket that flows from New to Closed. Strong fields, especially a clear subject and description, let any technician pick up the work. And the three big platforms, ServiceNow, Jira, and Zendesk, all share the same core ideas.
